lines.text: The smallest country in Central America, a land of volcanoes and coffee that has lived through massacre, civil war and sudden change. This is El Salvador.
Its story begins with Maya farmers. At Joya de Ceren, a volcano buried a whole village around the year six hundred, keeping it almost whole.
Nearby, the Maya built Tazumal, a city of stepped pyramids that stood for a thousand years.
In 1525 the Spanish founded San Salvador, and for three centuries ruled the land from Guatemala.
Independence came in 1821, and in 1841 El Salvador stood as a republic of its own. Coffee would soon make a few families very rich.
In 1917 Oscar Romero was born. As archbishop he would speak out for the poor, and pay with his life.
In 1932 peasants rose up, and the army answered by killing thousands. Salvadorans remember it simply as the Matanza, the massacre.
In 1969 tensions with Honduras boiled over around a football match, and the two countries fought a war of a hundred hours.
Ten years later civil war broke out between the government and the FMLN guerrillas. It lasted twelve years and took some seventy five thousand lives.
In 1981, in the middle of that war, Nayib Bukele was born. He would become president in 2019.
That same year the army entered the village of El Mozote and killed some eight hundred people, one of the worst massacres of the war.
In 1992, at Chapultepec in Mexico City, the two sides signed the peace that ended the war.
In 2001 El Salvador gave up its own money and made the American dollar its currency.
Twenty years later, under Bukele, it became the first country to make bitcoin legal money, while his war on the gangs jailed tens of thousands.
From buried villages to a nation remade, El Salvador's story is far from over.
